articles.headline: Vale, Bramble!
articles.text:
To the exclusion of other matter, we will give the main points of the connection of D. T. Bramble with the N. P. and Black Hills freight business.

Going clear back to the beginning, we will commence at the time when Dickinson offered a bonus to the firm of Kyes & Bramble to do their forwarding from there. Immediately after this offer was made, the firm came to Medora and tried to secure an advance in blood money from here. Their errand was profitless as no one would even enter into negotiations with them and they left town on a freight train swearing that they would never come here again, that they were sorry for even the amount they had laid out for dinner and they afterwards declared to Bob. Roberts that: "the Marquis and the whole d—— French army couldn't drag them to Medora." Bob. earnestly assured them that from the looks of things, no one seemed particularly stuck on their coming.

It must be that the Dickinson offer was finally accepted, as Bramble went to the Hills and began taking contracts with the merchants there for their freight via Dickinson.

Meantime, however, the Kyes end of the combination thought he saw a better thing in getting a large bonus of land in Belfield, starting a boom and unloading on tenderfeet. This plan worked to perfection as far as the bonus of land is concerned as, by the terms of the contract, the firm of Kyes & Bramble received a large slice of the Belfield townsite and adjacent country. This put another phase on the matter and Bramble immediately began making contracts via Belfield, pronouncing it far superior to the Dickinson route.

Meantime, considerable work had been done quietly for our route and when the Marquis and Joe Pennell went to the Hills it was agreed by the majority of the merchants to ship via Medora. Here, however, the mistake was made of appointing Bramble forwarder, notwithstanding the fact that he had said and done all he could against us.

Matters went along well enough for awhile, when complaints began coming in from the Black Hills merchants. One of these showed clearly the animus of Bramble toward our route. The regular charge is ten cents a hundred for forwarding and Bramble had agreed to the rate by accepting his position. Without any notice whatever, he began charging fifteen cents, an advance which made considerable difference in a large consignment. The merchants in at least one instance refused to pay the advance draft. This brought matters to such a crisis as Bramble thought was favorable and he went to Deadwood, leaving orders to reduce freighters rates to a dollar and fifty, thus causing all the freighters to strike and forwarding his own ends by thus trying to alienate the traffic of the Hills merchants. Just before leaving, Bramble remarked that there seemed to be some dissatisfaction in the Hills and that he intended to arrange matters satisfactorily, leaving and meaning to leave the impression with a society brother, that he intended to work for the best interests of our route.

For the reason that the Belfield contract was still in force, or that Bramble was intending all the time to sell out the N. P. route to Fred Evans, the latter being probably the case, negotiations had all the time been kept up in favor of some other route than that via Medora, as is shown by a telegram of Bramble's in reference to shipping the machinery for the Homestake 200-stamp mill, amounting to about 1,000,000 pounds. In this telegram he guarantees that he can quote low enough rates to secure she contract but that under no circumstances will he ship via Medora. Immediately after sending this telegram he went to St. Paul, met Fred Evans and it is reasonable to suppose, there concluded a deal with him as it was soon announced that Fred Evans had secured the contract. From this, the assumption was plain that Bramble had sold out the Medora route and nearly as plain that he even went back on Belfield.

This brings matters up to about the date when Bramble went to Deadwood five or six weeks ago, leaving with the promise we have mentioned above, of working for the Medora route. As his actions afterward showed, he intended all the time to betray our route and on account of the lack of explanation of several delays at this end of the line and the seeds of discontent he had sown in the Hills, there was a promising field for his traitorous operations.

Bramble thus had things all his own way in the Hills and for three weeks worked like a beaver convincing merchants that the Belfield route was the best one and inducing many to sign contracts via that point.

This was the state of affairs when the editor of the Cow Boy arrived in Deadwood. Relying on the promise Bramble had made, we were greatly surprised to find that he had been industriously engaged in giving the Medora route a black eye since his arrival. Naturally we inquired the points he had made against our route and found them in almost every instance to be unqualified lies. In the first place, he pronounced the route impracticable, a very favorite expression of his, by the way. In opposition to this we quoted the expressions of Messrs. John Sechler, J. Juelfs, Rassie Deffebach, Billy Brewer, L. H. Palmer, Dr. Louthan, Mr. Spear and many others, all of them well known in the Hills and all experienced in freighting and freight routes and they all say that the Medora route is the best one over which they have ever travelled.

Next, we were met by a direct lie on the part of Bramble. He claimed, and this repeatedly, that there was no depot at Medora and consequently no place to unload freight. Bramble's office is and has been in the depot here and no lapse of memory on his part can excuse the denial of the existence of one of the prettiest depots on the line. He can rest assured that this lie has done him no good in the Hills.

His next tale was more specious but fully as unconscionable. He stated that the Marquis had promised to build a freight house long ago but had failed in his promise. Bramble well knows that he, in company with the Marquis, examined the storage rooms on the slaughter house side-track and pronounced them equal to any demand until the fall freight began coming and to prove the uselessness of building a freight house, said that he had received word from Mr. Hannaford that until fall there need be no hurry about unloading the cars and that the goods could be transferred from them to the freighters wagons and thus avoid a second handling. He undoubtedly advanced these points to prevent the erection of a freight house here for two reasons. First, it would anchor the freight here where there was no chance of securing blood-money and second, because he wished to use the fact of there being no freight house here for the exclusive use of Black Hills freight, as a means to get merchants to ship to some other point where he could get blood-money.

Bramble also stated that the Marquis was financially embarrassed, that he had not the money to put on the stage line, that during his Hills trip the Marquis had fed the merchants on wind, that the Northern Pacific had "tumbled" to him, and that the N. P. officials had assured Bramble that he himself now "stood in" and that the Marquis had to take a back seat. That this is a mass of lies is already proven. The Northern Pacific has pooled issues with the Marquis and Mr. Bramble is "tapped" on the first deal. The N. P. inaugurated proceedings by buying a quarter interest in the Medora townsite and in conjunction with the Marquis have organized the N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co., with termini at Medora and Deadwood. This was accomplished less than a week ago and already the first fruits are visible here. Immense piles have been put in position and the sills laid for a freight house 240x42 feet. The work is being pushed vigorously by a large force of men, five additional workmen were put on this morning and still others will be added as soon as they can work to advantage. The climax of the whole thing, however, and where the N. P. S. & F. Co. hold four aces to Bramble's poor little bob-tail, is the fact of the Northern Pacific having refused rates on any other route than that via Medora.

The careful reader will have observed that we have passed by many disgraceful actions of this man Bramble, notably the one where he apparently joined forces with T. G. Jones in favor of our route, induced Jones to do the outside work of grading and bridging and then perfidiously made all his contracts by the way of Dickinson. But we do not need this and other facts to prove that Bramble has acted throughout, in a thoroughly unprincipled manner, and that he has repeatedly abused the confidence of the Hills merchants when at any time he could serve his ends in the slightest by so doing. That he has been a traitor to Dickinson and Medora is beyond question. That he entered into the whole business with the idea of making as much blood-money as possible and then selling out to Pierre is almost as certain. But the most certain thing of all is that Mr. Bramble's name is D-E-N-N-I-S.

And now that the matter is finally arranged, there will doubtless be no more trouble. In spite of the unavoidable delay in putting on the stages and the disgraceful actions of our thorn(?) in the flesh, the Black Hills merchants look hopefully to the Northern Pacific for relief from the extortionate rates of the Pierre route and for speedy railroad connection. This is bound to come soon and by the way of Medora.

Welcome, N. P. S. & F. Co.

Vale, Bramble!
articles.summary: Packard's editorial attacking freight forwarder D. T. Bramble for undermining the Medora–Black Hills freight route, and announcing the Northern Pacific's partnership with the Marquis de Morès in the new N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co.

articles.text:
The stockmen of Mason county, in Texas, have furnished 20,000 cattle to the spring drive at an average of $15 per head, making the handsome sum of $300,000.—[Colorado L. S. Record.

The Denver papers report sales of some Iowa and Missouri heifers, ones and twos, in that city at prices ranging from $30 to $35 per head. Of course they were well graded up, and their off-spring from good bulls, will be valuable.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped cattle-market items on the Texas spring drive and Denver heifer sales.

articles.text:
Kellogg & Co., have the largest horse ranch in Nevada, range 40 by 60 miles, and 2,000 horses grazing thereon.—[Reno Gazette.

A correspondent of the New Mexico Stock Grower reports the stampeding of a large herd of cattle near Devil's river, Texas, and the loss of about 2,000 head.

California breeders claim that they can import Hereford cattle at less cost from Australia than they can from England.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The special dispatch to the Drovers Journal from Liverpool quotes the cattle markets ½c higher; good to choice American steers 15@16c per pound dressed. Sheep weaker; best, 16c.

Two fence cutters were killed in the Territory near Medicine Lodge last week. The parties had been in the habit of going into the pasture, cutting posts, and on leaving would cut the wire or leave the gate open. Finally they were caught in the act, and on being remonstrated with by the cowboys, opened fire, which was returned, and both were instantly killed.—[Indian Chieftain.

It is not likely that many fat beeves will be ready for shipment from this country before August, though a few bunches that were fed until grass appeared may go out in July. Stockmen in this country have learned from experience that it does not pay to ship beeves before they are fat, and it is not likely there will be any mistake made this season. Fat cattle, of the grade this county turns out, always command top prices; if they are but half fat they as invariable sell below their value.—[Barber Co. Index.
articles.summary: Clipped range items from other papers: Nevada horse ranch, Texas stampede, Hereford imports, Liverpool markets, fence cutters killed, and beef shipping.

articles.text: The St. James ofttimes entertains among its numerous guests, men who represent great wealth in bovines as well as in mines. In this new West now-a-days a man's personal appearances do not by any means indicate his financial status. During the last few days of the week just passed there were congregated at the hotel a large number of eminent cattle growers from our own State, from Texas and New Mexico, whose combined wealth would represent millions. These cattlemen as a rule are quite unpretentious in their personal appearance. There is no glitter of diamonds about them, no ostentation. As a rule they are plain, practical, every day fellows, who make but little display of their worldly wealth. They buy and sell cattle by the tens of thousands as quickly as would an eastern farmer a single brute. Twenty, fifty, and even an hundred thousand is no gigantic transaction with many of those who come and go at the St. James. Wealth makes less display to-day than it did twenty years ago. The man with slouched hat and faded coat not infrequently has the longest bank account. He with glittering diamonds and the breast-plate too often is the shoddy. These thoughts were suggested on meeting ten or a dozen representative cattlemen in the rotunda of the hotel the other day. There was Mr. Wilkes, of the London Company, he who lately purchased the Wilson cattle and lands on the Republican for a sum of money greater than the worth of all the cattle of Colorado twenty years ago. Mr. Wilkes was a much plainer dressed man than the "roustabout" who tumbled the trunk in and out the hotel door. There was Mr. Pryor, the largest buyer of cattle the present year in Texas, and he whose 45,000 head of cattle now tramp the great trail leading up from the Lone Star state. He would easily be mistaken for a country merchant or a moderate farmer. The stout man with smiling face, whom everybody salutes, is Billy Wilson, the cowboy but yesterday, the cattle king to-day. Colossal fortune has not spoiled him. He is the same jovial fellow he was at the roundup. The plainly dressed man who just remarked to Mr. Pryor, "I'll take five thousand head if you'll shave the price a trifle," is Mr. H. H. Metcalf, whose word in the cattle markets is as good as Jay Gould's on Wall street. These stouter gentlemen on the outer rim of the circle are Messrs. Cranmar and Binkleman, the latter gentleman probably owning more ox-kind than any other man in America. That tall gentleman with a well-brushed hat and dude-like pants, is Captain Anderson, of the Coupalin ranch, in Colfax. He will wear different attire at the round-up. That stoutest of them all, that man who turns the scale beam at 250 pounds, avoirdupois, is Mr. George W. Thompson, of Trinidad. His cattle crop the grasses on a thousand hills, and his sheep are past counting. A shrinkage of one cent on beef might affect Thompson twenty thousand dollars. The young sprig with British look is young Ogilvy, of Greeley, son of the late Earl of Airlie. He is an importer of blooded cattle from the Highlands of Scotland, and a rising man in the cattle business.—[Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipped Colorado Live Stock Record sketch of wealthy but plainly dressed cattlemen gathered at the St. James hotel (Denver).

articles.text: A. M. Sinnott is in town on his way to Butte City.
articles.summary: A. M. Sinnott passes through Medora en route to Butte.

articles.text: Mollie Coleman has returned from Andrews station.
articles.summary: Mollie Coleman returns from Andrews station.

articles.text: The work train which had its headquarters at Sully Springs has gone to Allard.
articles.summary: The N.P. work train moves from Sully Springs to Allard.

articles.text: R. B. Downing, assistant road master has resigned and gone back to his old position on the Manitoba.
articles.summary: Assistant road master R. B. Downing resigns and returns to the Manitoba road.

articles.text: The many friends of conductor Clark will be glad to hear that he has resumed his old position on the road.
articles.summary: Conductor Clark resumes his place on the railroad.

articles.text: J. L. Truscott, Johnny Goodall and the cow-boys on the different round-ups are now in and preparations will soon be made for the beef round-up.
articles.summary: The spring round-up crews under Truscott and Goodall are in; the beef round-up is next.

articles.text: Bob Roberts' father died in Wales recently, leaving a considerable property to Bob, who will go over to receive it some time this fall.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts' father dies in Wales, leaving him property.

articles.text: Mr. O. C. Green, superintendent of telegraph and R. B. Wilson, special stock agent for the N. P., passed through here Wednesday, enroute for the west.
articles.summary: N.P. officials O. C. Green and R. B. Wilson pass through westbound.

articles.text: Joe Ferris returned from the east Monday evening, having purchased a large stock of groceries, which he will open in his new store room across the river.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris returns from the East with groceries for his new store across the river.

articles.text: The prospecting party which went down the river a few weeks ago, has gone back to the Hills, having found no pay gold, but good indications of silver and copper.
articles.summary: Prospectors return to the Black Hills after finding no pay gold down the Little Missouri.

articles.text: A tenderfoot got off the train an evening or two since and picking up a piece of scoria, gravely remarked: "This must be an awful country where the alkali cakes so solid."
articles.summary: Humorous item about a newcomer mistaking scoria for caked alkali.

articles.text: School has begun at the Cantonment school-house, with Dan. Williams teacher. Twenty scholars were enrolled the first day and there is every prospect of a successful session.
articles.summary: School opens at the Cantonment school-house with twenty pupils under Dan Williams.

articles.text: C. A. Spurling left last Saturday morning for Pierre to accept a position on the Northwestern, at an increased salary. We are glad to hear of his advancement but regret to see him leave.
articles.summary: C. A. Spurling leaves for a Northwestern railroad job at Pierre.

articles.text: Joe Pennell started with a car-load of mules yesterday morning for the Canadian Pacific, where some contracts have been taken by Tom Jones. It is not certain that Joe will stay and it is hoped that he will not.
articles.summary: Joe Pennell ships a car-load of mules to Canadian Pacific contract work.

articles.text: Judging from the success of the dance the evening of the 4th, the one to-morrow evening at the same place will be of a like nature. Roberts & Co. pledge themselves to the maintenance of the best order. All are cordially invited.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. announce another dance following the Fourth of July dance.

articles.text: P. D. Cravath, of Minneapolis, the editor's travelling companion to the Black Hills, continued his western trip Monday night. An account of the trip will be published in serial form, beginning with the next issue.
articles.summary: Packard's Black Hills travelling companion P. D. Cravath continues west; a serial account of the trip is promised.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin, of Mandan, held mass here Tuesday morning at Geo. Fitzgerald's, and Wednesday morning at the Marquis' residence. Father Martin takes Father Cassidy's place at Mandan, the latter now having charge of the Jamestown parish.
articles.summary: Father Martin of Mandan says mass in Medora, including at the Marquis de Morès's residence.

articles.text: Thanks to the able services of Messrs. Brewer, Houk, Palmer and Deffebach, there was no delay in issuing the Cow Boy during our absence, and as we have been repeatedly assured that the last two issues were the best since the initial number, our loss of a share of the glory is our subscribers' eternal gain.
articles.summary: Packard thanks those who issued the paper during his absence in the Black Hills.

articles.text: Mr. Gallup, of the New York law firm of Johnson, Gallup & Hurry, came through from the Hills with the pilgrims and is now at Wadsworth's ranch with Rassie Deffebach and Billy Brewer who are branding calves there. Mr. Gallup is making a careful study of the profits of stock raising and may conclude to invest.
articles.summary: New York lawyer Gallup, visiting Wadsworth's ranch, considers investing in stock raising.

articles.text: The coal taken from the Medora mine is pronounced by Geo. Wilkes, the ablest judge here, to be the best Bad Lands coal yet burned at the Company's works. He says it is especially rich in steam-giving properties. Messrs. Coleman & Brown and Mr. Z. Hyde also claim that it is superior to any lignite coal they have hitherto used for cooking. The coal is delivered for $2.50 a ton and considering this low price, business will be conducted on the cash on delivery basis. All orders will be taken at the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Medora mine coal judged the best Bad Lands coal yet; delivered at $2.50 a ton.

articles.text: The team of broncos which has occasioned so much difficulty again showed their untamable spirit last Monday. While George and Arthur Smith were hitching them up, they started to run away, pushing George, who was holding them by the bits, in front of them. He hung on until it seemed certain that they were about to run into the Cow Boy office when he jumped to one side and by great good luck, escaped uninjured. After the broncos were caught, a trot of twenty miles in a heavy lumber wagon, loaded with six men and five hundred pounds of sand scarcely tired them and they were as willing to run as ever. Large broncos, when tamed, make valuable work horses, but no one who is unacquainted with the breed can realize their wildness and the difficulty found in taming them in comparison to States' horses. It is exactly the difference between educating children who have enlightened parents and the children of aboriginal tribes.
articles.summary: A runaway bronco team nearly crashes into the Cow Boy office; George Smith escapes unhurt.

articles.text: Owing to the absence of the editor, the arrival of the Studebaker wagons, buckboards and platform spring wagons has not been chronicled. They are undoubtedly the best wagons manufactured and they will be sold at prices never before touched in this section. The best goods are always the cheapest and these are without question both superior in quality and lower in price than any others hitherto sold in the west. Call at the Cow Boy office and examine wagons and prices.
articles.summary: Studebaker wagons and buckboards have arrived for sale at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: D. K. Wade finished driving the cattle for the LeMoyne cattle company from Glendive to the home ranch on Tepee bottom, last Monday. The bunch consisted of 500 head of high grade heifers and were purchased from Mr. Mendenhall of Glendive. On his way east, Mr. LeMoyne purchased 200 head of thoroughbred one's and two's and a lot of Shorthorn bulls, which will soon arrive. Mr. Wade had good opportunities of judging the eastern Montana stock ranges and pins his faith stronger than ever to the Little Missouri Bad Lands. The gravel there has a tendency to make cattle foot-sore and numerous quicksands endanger their lives. The grass is also far better here and for protection in winter we are far ahead.
articles.summary: D. K. Wade completes a drive of 500 heifers from Glendive to the LeMoyne ranch on Tepee bottom.

Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Manager, P.O. Medora
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora
Brand: Pennell & Roberts, P.O. Medora — RR and JP on horses and mules
Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora — LSF
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., Howard Eaton, Manager, P.O. Medora — HK in circle
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Mont. — OX

articles.summary: Directory of display and cattle-brand advertisers on page 4; brand ads read mainly from the page view and match the prior issues' set.

events.date_basis: "less than a week ago" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Northern Pacific and the Marquis organize the N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co.
events.summary: The Northern Pacific bought a quarter interest in the Medora townsite and, with the Marquis de Morès, organized the N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co. running between Medora and Deadwood.
events.excerpt: The N. P. inaugurated proceedings by buying a quarter interest in the Medora townsite and in conjunction with the Marquis have organized the N. P. Stage & Forwarding Co., with termini at Medora and Deadwood.

events.date_basis: work under way at issue date; "this morning" refers to press day Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Freight house 240 by 42 feet begun at Medora
events.summary: Piles and sills were laid for a 240x42-foot freight house for Black Hills freight at Medora, with a large crew at work.
events.excerpt: Immense piles have been put in position and the sills laid for a freight house 240x42 feet.

events.date_basis: "five or six weeks ago" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: D. T. Bramble leaves for Deadwood and turns against the Medora route
events.summary: Packard charged that forwarder D. T. Bramble went to Deadwood promising to work for the Medora route, then spent weeks steering Black Hills merchants to the Belfield route.
events.excerpt: Bramble thus had things all his own way in the Hills and for three weeks worked like a beaver convincing merchants that the Belfield route was the best one

events.date_basis: Packard's Black Hills trip preceded his return; editor absent for the last two issues (Jul 3 and Jul 10)
events.title: Packard visits Deadwood and confronts Bramble's claims
events.summary: On his Black Hills trip Packard found Bramble had been disparaging the Medora route, and cited freighters who called it the best route they had travelled.
events.excerpt: This was the state of affairs when the editor of the Cow Boy arrived in Deadwood.

events.date_basis: issue date; standing notice
events.title: Stockmen offer $250 reward against grass fires
events.summary: The N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Continental Cattle Co., and other outfits offered $250 for the arrest of anyone setting grass fires in western Dakota's cattle country.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Culbertson & Weeks advertise reward for strayed horses
events.summary: Culbertson & Weeks of Keith offered rewards for four horses and ponies missing from Week's ranche on Beaver creek.
events.excerpt: All the above have hair brand of artist's palette with W in the centre, on left flank.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: A. M. Sinnott in Medora on way to Butte
events.summary: A. M. Sinnott was in town on his way to Butte City.
events.excerpt: A. M. Sinnott is in town on his way to Butte City.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Mollie Coleman returns from Andrews station
events.summary: Mollie Coleman returned from Andrews station.
events.excerpt: Mollie Coleman has returned from Andrews station.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: N.P. work train moves from Sully Springs to Allard
events.summary: The railroad work train headquartered at Sully Springs went to Allard.
events.excerpt: The work train which had its headquarters at Sully Springs has gone to Allard.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Assistant road master R. B. Downing resigns
events.summary: R. B. Downing resigned as assistant road master and returned to the Manitoba road; conductor Clark resumed his position.
events.excerpt: R. B. Downing, assistant road master has resigned and gone back to his old position on the Manitoba.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Round-up crews in; beef round-up to follow
events.summary: J. L. Truscott, Johnny Goodall and the cowboys of the round-ups came in, with the beef round-up to be prepared soon.
events.excerpt: J. L. Truscott, Johnny Goodall and the cow-boys on the different round-ups are now in and preparations will soon be made for the beef round-up.

events.date_basis: "recently" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Bob Roberts' father dies in Wales
events.summary: Bob Roberts' father died in Wales, leaving him a considerable property; Roberts planned to go over in the fall.
events.excerpt: Bob Roberts' father died in Wales recently, leaving a considerable property to Bob

events.date_basis: "Wednesday" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: N.P. telegraph superintendent and stock agent pass through
events.summary: O. C. Green, N.P. superintendent of telegraph, and R. B. Wilson, special stock agent, passed through Medora westbound.
events.excerpt: passed through here Wednesday, enroute for the west.

events.date_basis: "Monday evening" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Joe Ferris returns with groceries for new store
events.summary: Joe Ferris returned from the East with a large stock of groceries for his new store room across the river.
events.excerpt: Joe Ferris returned from the east Monday evening, having purchased a large stock of groceries

events.date_basis: "has gone back"; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Prospecting party returns to the Hills without pay gold
events.summary: A prospecting party that went down the Little Missouri found no pay gold but signs of silver and copper, and returned to the Black Hills.
events.excerpt: having found no pay gold, but good indications of silver and copper.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: School opens at the Cantonment school-house
events.summary: School began at the Cantonment school-house with Dan Williams as teacher and twenty scholars enrolled the first day.
events.excerpt: School has begun at the Cantonment school-house, with Dan. Williams teacher.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: C. A. Spurling leaves for Northwestern railroad post at Pierre
events.summary: C. A. Spurling left for Pierre to take a better-paid position on the Northwestern.
events.excerpt: C. A. Spurling left last Saturday morning for Pierre to accept a position on the Northwestern

events.date_basis: "yesterday" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Joe Pennell ships mules to Canadian Pacific work
events.summary: Joe Pennell left with a car-load of mules for Canadian Pacific contracts taken by Tom Jones.
events.excerpt: Joe Pennell started with a car-load of mules yesterday morning for the Canadian Pacific

events.date_basis: "the evening of the 4th" (July 1884)
events.title: Fourth of July dance at Roberts & Co.'s
events.summary: A successful dance was held on the evening of the Fourth.
events.excerpt: Judging from the success of the dance the evening of the 4th

events.date_basis: "to-morrow evening" after Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Dance announced at Roberts & Co.'s
events.summary: Another dance was announced for the following evening, with Roberts & Co. pledging good order.
events.excerpt: Roberts & Co. pledge themselves to the maintenance of the best order. All are cordially invited.

events.date_basis: "Monday night" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: P. D. Cravath continues west; trip serial promised
events.summary: P. D. Cravath of Minneapolis, Packard's companion to the Black Hills, continued west; an account of the trip was to begin in the next issue.
events.excerpt: An account of the trip will be published in serial form, beginning with the next issue.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" and "Wednesday morning" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Father Martin says mass at Fitzgerald's and the Marquis' residence
events.summary: Rev. Father Martin of Mandan held mass on Tuesday at Geo. Fitzgerald's and on Wednesday at the Marquis de Morès's residence.
events.excerpt: held mass here Tuesday morning at Geo. Fitzgerald's, and Wednesday morning at the Marquis' residence.

events.date_basis: issue date
events.title: Packard back; thanks staff who ran the paper in his absence
events.summary: Packard thanked Brewer, Houk, Palmer and Deffebach for issuing the Cow Boy while he was away.
events.excerpt: there was no delay in issuing the Cow Boy during our absence

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: New York lawyer Gallup visits Wadsworth's ranch
events.summary: Mr. Gallup of Johnson, Gallup & Hurry came from the Hills and was at Wadsworth's ranch studying stock raising with a view to investing.
events.excerpt: Mr. Gallup is making a careful study of the profits of stock raising and may conclude to invest.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Medora mine coal praised; sold at $2.50 a ton
events.summary: Geo. Wilkes judged Medora mine coal the best Bad Lands coal yet burned at the Company's works; it was offered at $2.50 a ton, orders at the Cow Boy office.
events.excerpt: The coal taken from the Medora mine is pronounced by Geo. Wilkes, the ablest judge here, to be the best Bad Lands coal yet burned at the Company's works.

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Runaway bronco team nearly hits Cow Boy office
events.summary: A bronco team bolted while George and Arthur Smith hitched it; George narrowly escaped injury near the Cow Boy office.
events.excerpt: they were about to run into the Cow Boy office when he jumped to one side and by great good luck, escaped uninjured.

events.date_basis: arrival not dated; week before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: Studebaker wagons arrive for sale at Cow Boy office
events.summary: A shipment of Studebaker wagons, buckboards and platform spring wagons arrived for sale at the Cow Boy office.
events.excerpt: the arrival of the Studebaker wagons, buckboards and platform spring wagons has not been chronicled.

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 17 Jul 1884
events.title: D. K. Wade completes LeMoyne cattle drive from Glendive
events.summary: D. K. Wade finished driving 500 high-grade heifers from Glendive to the LeMoyne cattle company's ranch on Tepee bottom; more cattle and Shorthorn bulls were coming.
events.excerpt: D. K. Wade finished driving the cattle for the LeMoyne cattle company from Glendive to the home ranch on Tepee bottom, last Monday.

events.date_basis: hearing date set in notice dated Jul 9, 1884
events.title: Land-office hearing set in Weber homestead contest
events.summary: John Weber contested a Billings county homestead entry for abandonment; parties were summoned to the Bismarck land office.
events.excerpt: the said parties are hereby summoned to appear at this office on the 21st day of August, 1884
